1:
The opening line answers the invitation closing the previous chapter, and Gill and Matthew Henry both think it should have been printed there. Henry makes the answer outdo the request: she called him her beloved, and he calls her his sister and spouse; she called the garden his, and he owns it — though of small account, yet it is mine — which Henry sets against the times when God disowned Israel and called their feasts theirs rather than his. Adam Clarke wants the verb in the past tense and the previous chapter's last clause carried down here, and reads the closing invitation as the bridegroom's words to his companions after the nuptial chamber, when the customary proofs of the bride's purity had been shown and the entertainment served; he rejects the reading that gives the words to the bride, since the verbs are plural. Charles Ellicott finds the difficulty in the same invitation and takes the margin as the key: what is drunk is the new strong wine of love, not the fruit of the grape, the poet inviting others into sympathy with his joy; he quotes Shelley to catch the feeling. Keil and Delitzsch read the exclamation as the union of love completing a betrothal, the God-ordained end of such love within the limits morality fixes. John Wesley and Gill hear Christ delighting in his people's obedience and bidding believers eat their spiritual food freely.

With the second verse the tone changes, and the voices divide over what kind of scene this is. Clarke doubts whether the passage down to the seventh verse is anything but a dream, and finds that supposition solves what is otherwise awkward — her hesitating to rise, his sudden disappearance, her being abroad in such disorder that the watch might well take her for a suspicious person. Ellicott says it outright: the poet pictures his lady dreaming, and the realities that hindered their union reappear in the fancies of sleep, so that when the hindrance is withdrawn she finds him gone. He compares the shut-out lover cold and wet with the dews of midnight to a well-known Greek lyric. Gill, Henry and Wesley take the sleep as a real declension rather than a dream. Gill is careful to say what it is not — not the dead sleep of sin, not a judicial slumber, but a frame unbecoming a saint, consistent with grace though grace is then little in exercise. Henry traces the decline: affections cooled, duty neglected, ease indulged; and observes that this sometimes follows more than ordinary enlargements, since even Paul was in danger of being puffed up by abundant revelations. Wesley has Christ knocking by his word and providence and Spirit at the door of the heart, and takes the dew on his head for what he suffered for the church.

The excuses that follow are handled on the same division. Clarke says the bride must have been dreaming or in real disorder of mind to make excuses so frivolous, and explains the second from the custom of washing the feet before lying down, adding a traveller's report of the same excuse still made where floors are of earth and shoes not worn indoors. Delitzsch fills in the picture from the words — she lies unclothed, and the washing implies she had gone barefoot through the day — and distinguishes the Hebrew word for the linen garment from the Arabic word for cotton, from which our own name for the cloth descends. Ellicott is content to gloss the garment as a tunic. Gill turns both clauses into the language of backsliding: the coat is the conversation she failed to keep, and the unwillingness to rise is an unwillingness to leave carnal ease for the trials following him would bring. Wesley reads them plainly as the objections of someone already settled for the night, to whom rising is merely inconvenient.
4:
Charles Ellicott gives the fullest account of what the hand through the opening does, and it governs his reading of the rest. The ancient lock, of a kind still used in the country, is a hollow bolt passing through a staple into the door-post, with movable pins dropping into matching holes when it is pushed home; the key slides inside the bolt and pushes the pins back so it can be withdrawn. In place of a key, an arm can be worked into the hollow bolt and the pins pushed up by hand, if the hand carries something soft to fill the holes and keep them from dropping again. Hence his explanation of the next verse: the lover, lacking a key, uses the myrrh he brought as a gift to try the lock, fails, and goes away, leaving the scent on the handle. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same place by etymology, deriving the word for the opening from a root meaning to break through and placing it not as a window but as the aperture pierced in the door above the bolt. Adam Clarke allows that if the scene were real the language would carry its married sense, but repeats that it bears every evidence of a dream. John Gill and John Wesley make the door the heart, the crevice a sign it was not wholly shut, and the hand efficacious grace, the finger of God, working inwardly on the conscience.

On the myrrh Delitzsch is technical: the second word means myrrh flowing of itself, breaking through the bark or running from an incision, the kind Pliny said none was preferred to; the lover has come perfumed as for a festival. Clarke prefers a custom, reporting that Roman brides were conducted to the bridegroom's house by torchlight and the door-posts anointed with fragrant oil, from which anointing he derives the Latin word for a wife, supposing the Jews may have kept the practice. Wesley draws the lesson that Christ, though withdrawing, left a sweet savour behind him. When the door is opened he is gone, and Delitzsch describes the sensation carefully: not the ecstasy of love, for then she would have flown to meet him, but a sinking of the soul such as the Latin poets describe, his voice striking her heart while the sense of her estrangement kept her from meeting him openly; he compares the disciples at Emmaus asking whether their heart did not burn while he spoke. Ellicott supposes an exclamation of disappointment from the departing lover, caught as she wakes. Wesley reads the withdrawal as just punishment for her earlier neglect.

The watchmen divide the readings sharply. Delitzsch keeps them literal — a real city patrol, rough men judging only by what is external, with neither eye nor heart for the grief of a loving soul, who struck the king's own bride as they would any common woman found abroad at night. He turns the detail that she searched in the city rather than the fields or villages into an argument against the theory that her beloved is a shepherd. Clarke reports the veil torn off rudely to discover who she was, and that in Eastern speech tearing a woman's veil means dishonouring her. Ellicott keeps to the garment, a light wrap thrown on for going out in haste, named once elsewhere. Wesley makes the watchmen the governors of the church, bound to comfort the faithful and discouraging them instead, and reads the loss of the veil as an attempt to represent her as having no relation to Christ. At the closing charge Delitzsch states plainly that all of this was dreamed, while insisting that the repentance and sense of separation it left entered her soul as deeply as waking experience; Gill has the church humbling herself to ask help of weaker believers; Clarke marks the end of the third day and night here.
9:
The question the daughters ask is taken by most voices as sincere. John Gill is emphatic that it is not scornful, not an attempt to shift off the trouble she laid on them, nor the question of people wholly ignorant of him, but of people wanting to hear more; Keil and Delitzsch agree that it cannot proceed from ignorance but exists to give her occasion to praise him aloud. Matthew Henry reports a harsher reading, that some take it as blame for making such ado about him, though he dwells rather on the beauty even slight acquaintance with Christ can see in those who bear his image. Charles Ellicott puts the verse to a different use: since love-poems describe the charms of the one addressed but not of the poet himself, a passage describing the bridegroom makes it nearly certain that the poem was sung as a wedding-song by alternating voices of maidens and young men, each praising one of the pair, as in the marriage poem of Catullus.

The general description is read at two levels. Gill takes the two colours for the two natures — white for a purity without mixture, on which he cites Cicero's remark that such a colour is chiefly becoming to God, and red for the flesh and blood he shares with his people — or both to the manhood, white for sinlessness and red for suffering; John Wesley agrees. Clarke keeps to complexion, red and white properly mixed making a fine one, and reads the next phrase literally as bearing the standard among ten thousand, or being one before whom a standard is borne, and so the chief; Ellicott notes the margin's reading. Delitzsch answers the objection that this is intolerable self-praise if Solomon wrote it: the words are not his own about himself but Shulamith's, and love idealizes — she sees him in her own transforming light.

From the head onward the description turns technical. Delitzsch distinguishes the two words for gold, the first fine gold guarded as a jewel, the second gold freed from baser metal, and reports the Aramaic rendering as gold that has stood the crucible's fire-proof. Gill collects rather than decides: some understand a diadem, others the hair powdered with gold dust in the manner Josephus records of the youths attending Solomon, a custom some Roman emperors afterwards used. Ellicott gives the curls two derivations, flowing or heaped up, and notes that the Greek and Latin versions read the word differently and rendered palm-leaves; Clarke suggests the crisped hair may be the moustache. Against all this Wesley protests, and his protest reaches the whole passage: we need not aim at a distinct application of these particulars to some special excellency of Christ, since such things are mere conjectures, the design being only to set him forth as one in whom there is no blemish from the crown of the head to the sole of the foot.

The eyes draw the most elaborate comment. Delitzsch takes the moist glancing of the eye for doves sipping beside a watercourse, the pupils seeming to bathe in milk as they swim in the white. Ellicott reports the received explanation of the last phrase, that the eye sits in its socket as a jewel in a ring's foil, granting it would suffice if the comparison were to the dove's own eye, which the turtle-dove rings with bright red skin; but he prefers to keep the bird bathing, its iridescence on the stream suggesting the quick loving glance, and quotes Keats and an Indian poem. Clarke explains the whiteness by the eastern use of a dark cosmetic, which gives the eye such lustre that a traveller said they seem to be swimming in bliss. Gill returns to allegory, taking the eyes for omniscience turned toward his people in mercy, not fierce but lovely; Wesley keeps to doves of a milk-white colour, chaste and pleasant.
13:
Whether the cheeks are the beard is the first question. Adam Clarke thinks so, and defends the thing: scarcely anything sets off a face better when kept in order, and he reports women who not only despised but execrated close-shaved Europeans. Charles Ellicott agrees the allusion is probably to a perfumed beard, noting the margin's towers of perfumes. John Gill reports the same reading from a Jewish commentator and many Christian ones, offering alongside it the cheek as the seat of blushing, and so of Christ's humility. Keil and Delitzsch keep to the face itself: the word for the bed comes from a root meaning to slope, and what is compared is the soft elevation of the cheek and the refreshing impression it makes. On the lips, Clarke says the flower may be any of the lily kind, whose tints come near a fine ruby lip; Ellicott quotes Tennyson.

At the hands the technical disagreement sharpens. Delitzsch rejects the lexicons' explanation that the figure is a closed fist whose stained nails are the gems: it is nowhere shown that Israelite women stained their nails with henna, still less men, and the word is not for palms but for hands, so the outstretched hand is meant. He takes the word rendered rings as a roller or cylinder, and Ellicott reaches the same reading, referring it to the rounded arm. Clarke and Gill keep the rings literal, Gill noting that this stone was worn on the fingers and stood in the high priest's breastplate. On the stone Gill collects the candidates — the best beryl resembles the colour of the sea, and the Hebrew word is used for the sea; others say chrysolite; others the jacinth — while Clarke prefers chrysolite and Ellicott suggests stones of Tarshish, chrysolite or topaz, said to have been first found in an ancient city of Spain. Clarke decides the next clause must mean a jewelled garment about the waist, since the literal sense — a white body with blue veins showing through — is plain enough but hardly what was intended.

Delitzsch pauses at the legs to state the principle governing the whole description: living beauty rendered in words rather than colours must borrow its figures from minerals and plants, and every such comparison must come short, because dead matter cannot fairly represent what is alive. He adds that the figure is anatomically just, the feet being the pedestal on which the bony pillars of the legs stand. Gill looks for the sense in dress: either the priestly linen garments, of thread six times doubled and so stiff and white as marble, or the eastern sandal bound with golden ribbons and adorned with gold, such as one Greek king is said to have worn. Clarke takes the golden sockets for slippers, on which ornament is still lavished in Asia, and reads the closing comparison plainly: as Lebanon lifts its head above the mountains near Jerusalem, so this man surpasses others. John Wesley keeps to brightness, comparing the feet to the fine brass of a later vision.

The last verse turns from the body to the voice. Delitzsch and Ellicott both insist the word is the palate, regularly named as the organ of speech, and Delitzsch rejects as fanciful the suggestion that it means the mouth for kissing; the point, he says, is that from speech the praise advances at last to the person himself. Gill will not choose among the senses, offering the words of the Gospel, the kisses of his mouth, the voice, and a rendering as taste. Clarke describes the close as a collapse of language: her metaphors exhausted, she can only say that the whole of him is loveliness. Wesley makes the same point in four words, glossing the summary as a refusal to run out into more particulars — of a piece with his protest against pressing each detail for a meaning.
